newsitem.title: USA: Stocks edge higher; bonds, dollar weaker.
newsitem.headline: Stocks edge higher; bonds, dollar weaker.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks edged higher Tuesday as the market rally was held back by a sell-off in technology shares, but bonds fell ahead of key inflation data later this week.
The dollar fell against most European currencies on jitters over the direction of German interest rates.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended up 9.31 points at 6,473.25 after racking up a mid-afternoon gain of nearly 50 points. On Monday, it surged 82 points.
The technology-laden Nasdaq Composite index was off 3.72 to 1,312.55, one day after closing at a new high.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,378 to 1,123 on active volume of 446 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
It was the second day of gains after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's cautionary comments about "irrational exuberance" in financial markets sent stocks into a tailspin Friday.

The Fed chief's words, which were interpreted to mean that the central bank might step in to cool things off by raising interest rates, sparked a sell-off Friday of 145 points in the Dow before it bounced back to end with a loss of 55 points.

"It's like Greenspan never said what he said. The spin on that is: It's one thing to use rhetoric and another to use policy," said Larry Wachtel, an analyst at Prudential Securities. "He's not going to bring the economy down by trying to stop IBM from going higher. It was a shot across the bow."
Earlier in the session, investors snapped up blue-chip stocks and semiconductor-related issues on an upbeat semiconductor book-to-bill report, which is a gauge of the industry's activity.

The November book-to-bill ratio rose to 1.15 from 1.11 in October, vs. expectations for a flat to slightly higher reading. The ratio means that manufacturers received $115 in new orders last month for every $100 in shipments.
The jump in technology stocks later evaporated on profit-taking.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond fell 11/32, or $3.44 on a $1,000 bond, raising its yield to 6.49 percent from 6.47 percent at Monday's close.
The dollar fell to 1.5530 German marks from 1.5580 marks late Monday. It edged down to 113.40 Japanese yen from 113.45 yen.
Oil prices declined after Iraq reponed a pipeline to resume oil exports after a six-year halt and suggested it would ratchet up sales.
Crude for January delivery fell 88 cents to $24.42 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange.

January heating oil dropped 2.51 cents to 69.62 cents a gallon, January gasoline sank 2.02 cents to 66.86 cents a gallon, while January natural gas rebounded to end up 17.4 cents at $3.396 per 1,000 cubic feet.
Coffee prices rose sharply in a technical correction to last week's slide to seven-week lows.
December coffee jumped 4.65 cents to 117.75 cents a pound at the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index closed 24.1 points higher at 4,035.7. In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 closed at 20,822.12, up 218.41 points or 1.06 percent.
